articles.text: Editor: I was shocked and frankly ashamed to read Joseph Gold’s “Seiji Ozawa a.k.a. the picture of Dorian Gray.” Although one need not slavishly follow the Latin maxim, “Of the dead, nothing but good is to be said,” I found Gold’s misguided attempt at “inside baseball,” with his entire focus on certain reportedly negative aspects of Ozawa’s musical career, to be in bad taste and certainly at odds with many of my own experiences of Ozawa’s music-making (for example, a stunning performance of Bartok’s Concerto for Orchestra, and one of his master classes for young conductors). A quick perusal of a number of obituaries of Ozawa will show how one can appropriately write about a career that was filled with many firsts, many high points, and, yes, the inevitable blemishes that can, in such a context, be mentioned. Gold suggests that Ozawa impressed only the “unsophisticated in the audience,” to which I would reply, “Please count me as unsophisticated.” –Tom Reicher

articles.text: Editor: I am writing in response to Joseph Gold’s brutish opinion piece about the recently deceased conductor Seiji Ozawa. As a member of the San Francisco Symphony for 32 years, I’ve had the opportunity to work with Mr. Ozawa as both a student at Tanglewood and as a professional in a couple of memorable returns he made to conduct the SFS. I always found him to be inspiring, supportive, engaging and professional. In particular, I fondly recall him coming in for one afternoon rehearsal and an evening concert of Beethoven’s 8th Symphony and Berlioz’ Symphonie Fantastique. Ozawa was well prepared, kind to the orchestra and, with his photographic memory, showed us everything he wanted and needed for the music through his elegant gestures with nary a word said. The orchestra rarely sounded as good and many of the Boston Symphony’s recordings from the Ozawa years are still favorites of mine both in terms of interpretation and sound. Most importantly, for Ozawa, it was never about him and always about the music. In the current era of social media where narcissism seems to be the norm, I look back on my own experiences with Seiji Ozawa as refreshing and truly special. –Jonathan Ring Grand Avenue 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Jay Russell PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Matt Simons, Lead reporter Ed Gilligan SCHOOLS Jay Russell SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: Editor: I am writing to provide more background regarding concerns about the recent use of the herbicide Ranger Pro, by the East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD) near the reservoir on Blair Avenue in upper Piedmont (see letter of January 31 and article of February 14). Ranger Pro contains glyphosate, the active ingredient in the herbicide Roundup. Glyphosate products such as Roundup are one of the most widely used weed killers in the world. About 200 million pounds of Roundup are sprayed on U.S. crops each year. It may persist in soil for an extended period with a typical half-life of about 7 weeks, but which can be up to 6 months depending on soil conditions. The CDC has reported that up to 80% of Americans have been exposed based on having traces of it in their urine. In 2015, the World Health Organization’s International Agency or Research on Cancer (IARC) identified glyphosate, the world’s most used herbicide, as a probable human carcinogen. In contrast, the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Scientific Advisory Panel (SAP) met in December 2016 to consider scientific evidence and concluded that it was not likely to be carcinogenic if used as recommended. There were significant methodological differences in the reports contributing to the different results. In February 2020, the EPA published an interim decision which stated that there were no risks of concern to human health when glyphosate was used according to the label instructions. This decision was challenged in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit and was vacated by the Court in July 2022 meaning that Court concluded that there were insufficient data to support the position that glyphosate did not adversely affect human health. Whatever the EPA position on glyphosate, it is notable that nearly $11 billion was awarded in 2022 to settle approximately 100,000 cases against Monsanto, the original manufacturer of Roundup until it was sold to Bayer in 2018, and there have been subsequent significant financial settlements. The potential adverse health effects of glyphosate include cancer, most notably non-Hodgkins’s lymphoma (NHL). The American Cancer Society estimates that in 2024 there will be more than 80,000 new cases of NHL in the United States and that more than 20,000 people will die from this cancer. It is one of the more common cancers of children, teens, and young adults. Glyphosate is a toxin for the nervous system. Recent reports suggest that glyphosate exposure may be associated with a higher overall risk of death. Exposure to glycoside in early childhood was recently shown to be associated with the development metabolic syndrome in late teenage or early adult years. Metabolic syndrome is a complex of heart disease risk factors which accelerate the development of heart disease, the leading cause of death in the U.S. At the city level, Piedmont’s Integrated Pest Management Plan (IPM) prohibits the use of glyphosate products. Glyphosate products are legal in California and State law does not allow the City to ban the use of these products by other entities (private property owners, including EBMUD) within Piedmont’s jurisdictional boundaries. So, what should we do about glyphosate? First, Roundup and other glyphosate products should be viewed as serious health hazards and their use and exposure to them should be avoided as much as possible. Second, the City should be proactive in discouraging its use by EBMUD and other private property owners in Piedmont. The State of California maintains a helpful website on integrated pest management (https://ipm.ucanr.edu/GENERAL/pesticides.html), a set of practices which minimize the use of herbicides. Requests for a reference list can be sent to me at ssidney3203@ gmail.com. Dr, Stephen Sidney, MD, MPH, is a 40-year Piedmont resident and retired epidemiologist with Kaiser Permanente Northern California. articles.text: Editor: The mayor has proposed that all 132 apartments allocated by the new Housing Element to the Moraga Canyon planning area be built in Blair Park. These would include 62 units for low, very low, and extremely low-income families. She proposes this despite the fact that Blair Park is a former un-engineered landfill enclosed on 3 sides by impassable terrain and on the 4th by a major arterial that an earlier, city-commissioned EIR found unavoidably dangerous to access or cross due to sight lines shorter than those considered safe by Caltrans. Given that EIR, the Mayor’s proposal violates existing city policy that all new construction provide safe sight lines. When reminded of this violation, city staff responds that the Council need not acknowledge the prior EIR because the project it described was not approved. This response misleads Piedmont residents and the Council. The prior EIR found not only that Piedmonters would be put at risk by short sight lines if the then proposed project were approved, but also that the alignment of Moraga Avenue allows no access to Blair Park that meets Caltrans safety standards. That alignment has not changed. The mayor does not acknowledge that her proposal violates city policy by putting Piedmonters in unavoidably unsafe circumstances. But I plead with the remainder of the Council, and with our professional staff, to acknowledge that housing 132 families in Blair Park will not only physically and socially segregate those families from the remainder of Piedmont, but also put all of us who use Moraga Avenue in circumstances that neither Caltrans nor city policy deem acceptable. –Ralph Catalano, Ph D

Measure F is a continuation of Piedmont’s City Services Tax, which funds core city services. This measure has been approved by Piedmont voters continuously since 1981. All funds raised stay in Piedmont, to support our public safety, parks, greenspaces, stormwater infrastructure, streets, and public facilities. Piedmont looks and works as well as it does because of community support of this essential revenue source. The City of Piedmont takes a conservative and transparent approach to annual budgeting, constantly reviewing, monitoring, prioritizing and projecting ahead for the next ten years. Ranger Pro contains glyphosate, the active ingredient in the herbicide Roundup. Glyphosate products such as Roundup are one of the most widely used weed killers in the world. About 200 million pounds of Roundup are sprayed on U.S. crops each year. It may persist in soil for an extended period with a typical half-life of about 7 weeks, but which can be up to 6 months depending on soil conditions. The CDC has reported that up to 80% of Americans have been exposed based on having traces of it in their urine. In 2015, the World Health Organization’s International Agency or Research on Cancer (IARC) identified glyphosate, the world’s most used herbicide, as a probable human carcinogen. In contrast, the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Scientific Advisory Panel (SAP) met in December 2016 to consider scientific evidence and concluded that it was not likely to be carcinogenic if used as recommended. There were significant methodological differences in the reports contributing to the different results. In February 2020, the EPA published an interim decision which stated that there were no risks of concern to human health when glyphosate was used according to the label instructions. This decision was challenged in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit and was vacated by the Court in July 2022 meaning that Court concluded that there were insufficient data to support the position that glyphosate did not adversely affect human health. Whatever the EPA position on glyphosate, it is notable that nearly $11 billion was awarded in 2022 to settle approximately 100,000 cases against Monsanto, the original manufacturer of Roundup until it was sold to Bayer in 2018, and there have been subsequent significant financial settlements. The potential adverse health effects of glyphosate include cancer, most notably non-Hodgkins’s lymphoma (NHL). The American Cancer Society estimates that in 2024 there will be more than 80,000 new cases of NHL in the United States and that more than 20,000 people will die from this cancer. It is one of the more common cancers of children, teens, and young adults. Glyphosate is a toxin for the nervous system. Recent reports suggest that glyphosate exposure may be associated with a higher overall risk of death. Exposure to glycoside in early childhood was recently shown to be associated with the development metabolic syndrome in late teenage or early adult years. Metabolic syndrome is a complex of heart disease risk factors which accelerate the development of heart disease, the leading cause of death in the U.S. At the city level, Piedmont’s Integrated Pest Management Plan (IPM) prohibits the use of glyphosate products. Glyphosate products are legal in California and State law does not allow the City to ban the use of these products by other entities (private property owners, including EBMUD) within Piedmont’s jurisdictional boundaries. So, what should we do about glyphosate? First, Roundup and other glyphosate products should be viewed as serious health hazards and their use and exposure to them should be avoided as much as possible. Second, the City should be proactive in discouraging its use by EBMUD and other private property owners in Piedmont. The State of California maintains a helpful website on integrated pest management (https://ipm.ucanr.edu/GENERAL/pesticides.html), a set of practices which minimize the use of herbicides. articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department will launch a new online crime map through its portal on the City of Piedmont website on March 1. The new public-facing database will allow citizens to view the latest crime data in their neighborhoods and will also support new features such as custom alerts and notifications. The police department hopes that the newer, easier-to-use crime map will increase citizens’ awareness and promote greater transparency between PPD and members of the public. “The public wants to know what’s going on in their community and we want them to know what’s going on,” said Lisa Douglas, Support Services Commander at PPD. “It’s important to have that information available in a consumable and user-friendly way so that it builds trust and engagement.” Until recently, the PPD hosted its crime map on City Protect, another dedicated crime map website. However, problems with the system prompted the department to look at alternative providers. “We received complaints from the public about both [City Protect] itself being unresponsive and stopping its email notifications,” said Douglas. She also alluded to problems the department had with the previous software provider, including unexpected loss of connection. “It just didn’t perform satisfactorily for us,” Douglas added. The Department has not updated its crime map on City Protect since October 17, 2023, due partially to difficulties the department had using it. PPD will host the new crime map via Citizen Connect, a map-centric portal developed by tech company Tyler Technologies that specializes in allowing public agencies to view and analyze development trends in their area. The new crime map will also boast new features like custom alerts and notifications which can be set by users, as well as refined data tools, like the ability to draw a polygon around a certain neighborhood and find out what kind of activity is happening in that area. Upon its launch the crime map will have three months of data available from the police department’s computer-aided dispatch (CAD) and records management systems (RMS). Tyler Technologies is also the vendor for the CAD and RMS at the police department, which the department has said will make integrating their information into the new crime map even easier. The police department does not have a URL available for its crime map yet, but it plans on releasing a link to it through the City’s communication channels by its launch date.
articles.title: Police Dept. to launch new online crime map

articles.text: After it rains, sometimes we get the chance to see a rainbow in the sky. But what causes a rainbow to form? Rainbows are created when sunlight is refracted by water droplets in the sky, resulting in a colorful display for us to observe. Did you know that this phenomenon can also be seen at night? However, instead of a rainbow, it is known as a moonbow. What causes a Moonbow? A moonbow is produced by the same process that forms a rainbow, with the Moon acting as the light source instead of the Sun. Earlier this year, observers were able to witness a moonbow in Oakland. When the right conditions align, it is a stellar sight to witness. However, such sightings are rare. Why is a Moonbow rare? Moonlight is significantly fainter than sunlight, which is why the circumstances in which you can see a moonbow, especially one with color are so rare. For a moonbow to appear, specific conditions must be met: a full or nearly full Moon, light rain, or sufficient moisture in the atmosphere to refract light, and clear skies to allow the Moon’s light to shine through. What if the moon is not completely full? A moonbow may still appear, but instead of displaying the typical colors we are familiar with, the moonbow will appear white or grey. While rainbows color our daytime sky, moonbows bring magic to our nighttime sky. They show us that even simple things like sunlight, moonlight, and raindrops can create something truly spectacular! articles.text: The benches outfront of Wildwood Elementary and a new safer landscaping layout were dedicated to retired Principal Carol Cramer and Administrative Assistant Christine Petersen on Friday, February 16. A crowd of 40 people were on hand to honor the decades of service from Cramer and Petersen and to hear about the improved safety of the pick up area. First year Wildwood Principal Melissa Daymond opened the ceremony with a heartfelt message about the special team Cramer and Petersen were and the robust role they played in shaping the culture and community at the school and throughout the district. Cramer and Petersen both, started at PUSD in 1988, and both spoke to the crowd before cutting the big purple ribbons over the benches. Cramer emphasized it’s the relationships that make a place and make a community. Wendi Sue was the designer on the safety project, which made landscaping changes focused on making it easier for parents and children to see and find one another at the Wildwood pick up zone. Overgrown manzanita bushes had obstructed visibility and made for more challenges during pick up. Children can now safely sit on the benches after school while waiting for their caretakers to pull upfront. The garden space is now planted with native drought tolerant plants that are filling in the space. The Wildwood Parents Club (WPC) collaborated with the Dad’s Club and had the support of a private donor to make this project possible. School Board member Cory Smegal also paid tribute with a few well placed remarks about her family’s journey through Wildwood and the monumental impact made by Cramer and Petersen. Last year’s WPC President, Xenia Meyer, explained the process of the project at the event and detailed how WPC and Dad’s Club collaborated to support this safety project. “Our retired Principal Carol Cramer and Administrative Assistant Christine Petersen worked alongside one another for so many years; it is so fitting that there are benches side by side in their honor,” said Meyer. Wildwood School principal for previous 23 years Carol Cramer (left) sits with new principal Melissa Daymond.
articles.title: Wildwood School dedicates benches to Carol Cramer, Christine Petersen

articles.text: The Wildwood Dads Club hosted a crowd of more than 130 guests at their 37th annual Crab Feed on Saturday, February 10, in the Veterans Hall. Guests at the adults-only event paid homage to the 100th anniversary of Wildwood Elementary School by dressing in the style of the roaring 1920s. Volunteer parents decked out the venue in twenties era gold and black decorations, with old Piedmont news clippings on the walls and tables. A champagne tower greeted guests upon entry to the hall. Orleans spicy spinach, Tunisian spiced corn, scalloped potatoes, macaroni and cheese, garlic bread, and a tossed salad. “The food was amazing, I went back for thirds it was so good,” said Carolyn Pan, co-President of the Wildwood Parents Club. Two student bands provided live music, the Freshmen Jazz Combo and Juvenoia. Wildwood dad and DJ Ben Anderson kept the party going until the 11 p.m. closing time. Everyone had a blast snapping pictures in the Photo Booth too. It took 20 volunteer dads, 10 sponsors and 250 pounds of crab to pull off this event. “The most important thing about this event is how it brings the community together. For me, it was a wonderful way to enjoy a delicious dinner out with my wife, surrounded by friends and fun,” said Jake Strzelecki With nearly everyone buying into the flapper or pageboy aesthetics, Wildwood Principal Melissa Daymond outdid them all by donning the famed crab suit at the event. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. articles.text: The Highlanders soccer season came to an end on Friday, February 16 at Witter Field, falling 3-1 to No. 7 Archie Williams in the Division 3 North Coast Section. PHS, the No. 3 seed, allowed all three goals in the first 25 minutes and scored their lone goal minutes before halftime. PHS ends its season with a 12-3-3 overall record in its first season in Div. 3 after being promoted last year. The visiting Peregrine Falcons played a composed game defensively, celebrating every tackle and clearance for 80 minutes. Their energy and momentum was impressive. “The difference was the intensity of the teams,” said PHS coach Todd Sullivan. “They came out really hungry and were the better team. They worked harder from the opening whistle and were more organized. The early goals hurt and those were our mistakes. We had a mountain to climb at 0-3,” he added. “They are obviously an organized side. The coach has been there awhile and they have big, strong boys. They knew how to stay organized and close out a game,” said Sullivan. Piedmont has some key players graduate this year: goalie Axel Saldanha, defenders Ben Elmquist and Andrew McLaughlin, striker Oliver Shafroth, captain midfielder Riley Stratman, and captain and four-year starting striker Aiden Woolwine. However a wealth of talent returns next season: forwards Bosco Lorin and Gianluca Bini, midfielders Jake and Logan Faucher, and Harper Mand, fullback Niko Markopoulos, fullback/ winger Jacques Saldanha, and central attacker Enzo Bernales, who was the Post’s Sophomore of the Year in 2023. 3-1 loss to Archie Williams Archie Williams struck first in the 5th minute on a botched linkup. A pass back was mishandled and rolled to the Falcons’ left winger, who slotted it in. Three minutes later, the visitors drew a free kick slightly past midfield, and disaster struck again for Piedmont. This time, a long ball into the box was allowed to fall near the right post, settling nicely for an Archie Williams forward to score easily. Jacques Saldanha had a chance for Piedmont in the ninth minute after locating a long ball over the top and taking a shot that went high. AWHS’ goal keeper came out of net to challenge Jacques’ shot, colliding with the PHS winger but there was no call. Bernales also had a shot on target from a free kick a few yards above the penalty area, but the Falcons’ keeper was there. That chance led to a counterattack from Archie Williams, leading to a penalty awarded to the visitors after a collision in the box. The Peregrine Falcons’ initial PK attempt was saved by Axel Saldanha, but the shot deflected back to the penalty-taker for a goal in the 25th. Score 3-0. Stratman had a shot hit the crossbar in the 37th, while Logan Faucher had a header go wide in the 38th. Piedmont scored from a corner in first-half stoppage time when a cross into a crowded area was pushed home by Mand. In the second half, Piedmont had chances from Logan Faucher Staff Photos Piedmont exited the North Coast Section playoffs after falling to Archie Williams, 3-1. Pictured is Oliver Shafroth surrounded by defenders. Enzo Bernales makes a play against a defender. He scored twice in the first round against Novato.

We had them on the ropes at times,” said PHS coach Dan Chubbock. Piedmont had its chances to score, including a penalty kick that was stuffed with around 10 minutes left in the game. “We kept it tight and created a few chances. It was a very endto-end game. We had the better of the opportunities in the second half. We won a penalty for a handball in the box, but their keeper made a really athletic save and tipped it onto the crossbar. Making a difference in Friday’s game was the absence of two critical starters out with injuries – forward Lola Beihn, and talented midfielder Juliana Thornborrow who left the game after 15 minutes. “We lost Juliana, who came off injured, and we were without Lola as well. The players who were out there did great. It could’ve gone either way. I was proud of their performance,” Chubbock said. 2-0 loss to Cardinal Newman Cardinal Newman struck in the 8th minute into the first half after connecting with a header goal on a cross into the box from a corner. Then around the 46th minute in the second half on a rare Olimpico, where the Cardinals’ corner-kick taker bent her cross into the net at the far post. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s baseball team returns to Humphries Diamond for the spring season. Piedmont’s baseball team is back for the spring season, starting with a game at St. Mary’s in Berkeley this Saturday, February 24. The Highlanders went 14-11 last year in their first season in the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division. It caught everyone’s attention in the Division 4 North Coast Section playoffs, advancing to the semifinals as the No. 8 seed. They lost a 11-10 barnburner against No. 5 Justin-Siena after upsetting No. 1 Fortuna 5-2 the previous round. The team lost key players to graduation, notably Michael Aikawa and Ryan McConathy. But a strong cast of players should provide a potent batting lineup. Returning starters include outfielder Markos Lagios, shortstop/ pitcher Peter Krumins, catcher Will Parker, outfielder/pitcher John Olsen, former first-baseman Dimitri Papahadjopoulos, infielder Diego Delventhal, and versatile utility players Brandon Dicke, and Ellis Moss. “We have 23 kids on the roster, so we’re going to need everyone. Players will have to play multiple positions and try positions they aren’t comfortable in just yet,” explained coach Eric Olson. Lagios was the Post’s Honorable Mention for 2023 Sophomore of the Year after batting .303 with 23 hits, 11 doubles, three triples, and 18 RBIs, He led the team with two home runs and 27 runs scored. “Markos is going to play center field and will lead off for us,” Olson said. “Peter could hit second and Will Parker will hit third; he’s going to be a stud.” Krumins s committed to play baseball for Northern Kentucky next year, takes over at shortstop for Aikawa and will be a pitcher. “We lost our ace last year with Michael Aikawa. He wasn’t a pitcher but he did a great job when we asked him. Peter Krumins can certainly do it,” Olson said. Delventhal was another player who impressed in the second half of the season. He’ll be a fulltime starter at second base. He was named Honorable Mention for 2023 Freshman of the Year after appearing 14 times for nine hits, two RBIs and three runs scored. In the NCS play offs, he had two hits, a run scored and an RBI against Justin-Siena. Olson is doing some mixing and matching to create a threeman starting pitching rotation. Krumins will get time as the No. 1 option, along with John Olsen, Papahadjopoulos, Seve Sanchez, and Ellis Moss, all with experience from last season. “Peter will throw, John Olsen is going to help out there, Dimitri Papahadjopoulos, Ellis Moss and Seve Sanchez will all get time and are all seniors. We’re hoping those five kids can step up,” Olson said. Piedmont plays its first game at St. Mary’s this Saturday at 1:00 p.m. before their home opener at Humphries Diamond against Encinal on Thursday, February 29 at 3:30 p.m. Peter Krumins, a senior leader, will be playing shortstop and pitching. Markos Lagios, a junior, enters his third year as a starter.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s track and field team is back in action for another spring season. They competed in the Grizzly Invitational on Saturday, February 17 at San Lorenzo High School. Piedmont’s boys team finished first and the girls’ team was second. The Highlanders are the last team to be displaced by the prolonged renovations of Witter Field. Their last roster of 110 athletes has had to split time training at Laney College, Witter Field, and running the streets of Piedmont. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team returns to Witter Field after finishing 8-8 last season. Coach Carlton Chan said he had the largest turnout of players during his time at the school. He will be assisted by a former player, Kate Abel (PHS Class of 2019), who will coach the junior varsity team. “We have a lot of new kids, it’s probably the largest team I’ve ever had. We have 18 on varsity and the rest on JV. We have Kate Abel, who was an assistant coach last year, is now head coach of the JV team. She’s a former Piedmont athlete, played at Chapman, and is now coming full-circle,” coach Carlton Chan said. Last year’s team lost several key players to graduation: attacker Molly Ashton, goalie Lindsay Kottle, and middie/ attacker Eleanor Lavin. Lavin earned honors by being selected for the U.S. Lacrosse’s NorCal Senior All Star Game. This year’s team will include Ruby Guzdar as the incumbent leading scorer, Hailey Marshburn, goalie Friedie Schickedanz, and Jane Hempeck, Peyton Watson, Chloe Graham, and Luisa Cole. Guzdar has been named a team captain, along with Hempeck. “We have a lot of returners and we’re happy about that. I think they’re going to make a big impact. Jane will make a big impact on the defensive side and we’ll also get Hailey Marshburn back from soccer. She has a strong voice and is very good,” Chan said. Schickedanz played goalie last season, but will see more action in the field this year. “Now that Molly [Ashton] has graduated, Friedie is going to anchor that position. We’ve been trying to groom her to take that spot and she’s gotten pretty good,” Chan said. Watson is another young player who got time as a freshman and has been making her mark in training. “Peyton Watson is someone we’re excited about, she’s just gotten better and better. As a freshman, we saw glimmers of her ability and now she understands she’s faster, bigger, and stronger. In practice, she’s showing she can really take it to the hole. She’ll move around,” Chan said. Junior Annika Hattan-Kutter will debut as the starting goalRuby Guzdar is a captain and the leading returning scorer from last season. keeper. “Annika will get her first season as starting goalie. I told her, it’s the goal to be the starter and she needs to own it. She has a great attitude and is a good goalie. I think she can handle it,” Chan said. Chan is hopeful that this year’s team will emulate some similar aspects to Piedmont’s NCS Championship-winning team of 2020, which featured a lot of movement and cuts toward the net. “The good thing is, most of everyone are returners and understand the offense. We’re going to run a similar offense to where we’re cutting left and right. We’re going to bring back some offense from our NCS Championship days,” Chan said. Piedmont starts its season on Wednesday, February 28 at Dublin. Hailey Marshburn is a returner and a four-year starter.

articles.text: South African artist Zanele Muholi The first major exhibition of South African artist Zanele Muholi on the West Coast is now on view at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, and will be available for viewing through August 11. The multimedia exhibition, entitled Zanele Muholi: Eye Me, features over 100 of the artist’s photographs from 2002 to the present alongside paintings, sculpture and video. Eye Me celebrates the artist’s Black queer community in post-Apartheid South Africa and showcases issues of gender identity, representation and race. Muholi was born in Durban and currently lives and works in Johannesburg, South Africa. The museum has featured works by Muholi in the past, including Faces and Phases in the 2011 exhibition Face of Our Time. Their work was also featured in Public Intimacy: Art and Other Ordinary Acts in South Africa, co-organized by SFMOMA and the Yerba Buena Center for Arts in 2014. To learn more and to purchase passes to the museum, visit https://www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/zanele-muholi-eye-me/.

articles.text: Theatre to host community night this Friday Photo by Kevin Berne Ixtlán and Oogie Push appear in Aurora Theatre Company’s production of Manhatta. Aurora Theatre Company’s current production of Manhatta is playing onstage now through March 10. The play by Mary Nagle follows two stories separated by centuries and focuses on the native Lenape people. The island of Manhattan in New York City was once known as Manahatta by the Lenape. The Dutch West India Company established a trade route with the native people in the 17th century but soon began to bargain for the island itself, effectively pushing out the Lenape tribes. Centuries later, a similar scenario plays out in the New York City housing market when inflated housing prices force out longtime city dwellers. Once again, greed causes many to lose their homes. Director Shannon Davis weaves the two narratives into a single story of avarice and loss through the eyes of a young Lenape woman, Jane Snake, who returns to her ancestral homeland. The cast includes Linda Amayo-Hassan as Bobbie, Livia Gomes Demarchi as Le-le-wa’ -you/Jane, Max Forman-Mullin as Jakob, Anthony Fusco as Peter Minuit, Ixtlán as Se-ket-tu-mayqua and Oogie Push as Toosh-kipa-kwis-i. A discussion of Manahatta will be hosted after the show on Friday, February 23, and Wednesday, February 28. An indigenous community night will also be held this Friday, February 23. featuring guest speaker and Ohlone healer Kathleen Grace. A pre-show reception will be held at 6 p.m. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.auroratheatre.org/index. php/shows-events/20232024- season/Manahatta, or call the box office at 510-843-4822. The theater is located in downtown Berkeley at 2081 Addison Street.

articles.text: San Francisco Opera continues its Schwabacher Recital Series with an evening performance on Wednesday, March 2. Tickets are available now. The recital series offers audiences an opportunity to hear upcoming gifted singers in an intimate setting. Since 1983, the series has featured renowned artists and has been instrumental in launching international careers. The evening’s performance features soprano Arianna Rodriguez, soprano Olivia Smith, mezzo-soprano Nikola Printz, bass-baritone Jongwon Han, and pianist Yang Lin. The artists will perform in a program curated by American tenor Nicholas Phan entitled The Secret Garden, composed of songs in English, German, Russian, Spanish, French and Korean. “Throughout the ages, poets and composers have been Mezzo-soprano Nikola Printz inspired by nature, finding meaning and metaphor for the human experience through our relationship with the flora and the fauna that surround us,” said Phan. “In this spirit, The Secret Garden is a bouquet of song, featuring songs by beloved composers such as Margaret Bonds, Lili Boulanger, Henry Thacker Burleigh, Ernest Chausson, Aaron Copland, Edvard Grieg, Franz Schubert, Richard Strauss and Ralph Vaughan Williams.” The concert begins at 7:30 p.m. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfopera.com/seasons/schwabacher-recital-series/. articles.text: All art is introspective to some degree, but some pieces ask us to stop and reflect more than others. A woman sitting in a boat without oars contemplates her reflection. A red finch, frozen in an explosion of water from its’ bird bath. A wedding. A stormy night. A pair of hands reach toward heaven holding phones. This invitation to reflect is the goal of an exhibition titled “Moments that Give Pause,” now on display at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The show brings together the work of four Easy Bay artists, Carol Aust, Debra Collins, Leslie Vail Crisfield, and Gretchen McCondochie, all united by a theme of contemplating beauty. The artists worked in Artists Carol Aust (left), Debra Collins, Leslie Vail Crisfield, and Gretchen McCondochie a range of mediums and materials to bring the display to life, including traditional painting, Dawn by Debra Collins is an example of the artist’s work using cut paper. sewn fiber and cut paper. “I do figurative paintings of people traveling through emotional landscapes,” said Aust, an Oakland-based painter. Her paintings vary between depictions of intimate moments of beauty between family and lovers to lone figures in solitary situations. “I want all of my paintings to have a degree of mystery. I want the viewer to be able to look at it and have their own opinion of what each piece means,” she said. Leslie Vail Crisfield leans more heavily into her sense of solitude for her work. “I often travel and take myself on solo art retreats for my work. I’ve been to Joshua Tree by myself for a month, Sedona by myself. I just put myself in the car and go,” she said. This quality appears in her work through landscapes that use black and white to evoke a sense of seclusion and natural beauty. “I usually wind up with these stark light and dark things,” she said. Moments that Give Pause will be open for viewing on Saturdays and Sundays, February 17 through March 3 from noon to 3 p.m. Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue at the corner of Bonita Avenue. In Carol Aust’s Reflection, a woman sits calmly in a boat without oars, contemplating her image in the water. Gretchen McCondochie’s “Embroidered Bird” Splash 1 (left) and Splash 2 by Leslie Vail Crisfield depict an explosion of water in a birdbath.
articles.title: “Moments That Give Pause” art show at Center for the Arts

The works of J.S. Bach (Chaconne fr. Partita #2), Hector Villa-Lobos (Prelude #1), Isaac Albeniz (Asturias), and Francisco Tarrega (Recuerdos de la Alhambra) will be performed. articles.text: Two Blocks in Rome: Bernini, Borromini, and Via del Quirinale Local artist and art historian Michael Stehr returns to Piedmont Center for the Arts on March 9 for another spirited foray into the world of art history. For this next adventure, Stehr takes the audience to his beloved Rome to consider one of his favorite walks: a two-block stretch along the Via del Quirinale. The highlight of this stroll is the unique ability to compare, practically side by side, major architectural achievements by two founders of the Italian Baroque style: Gian Lorenzo Bernini and Francesco Borromini. While both are regarded as founders of the same artistic movement, the two could not be more different as individuals. These personal differences are clearly manifested in their drastically contrasting aesthetics. Bernini’s more theatrical style is demonstrated at the first stop on the journey, at the small church of Sant’Andrea al Quirinale. After traveling a mere 100 yards, one stands at the door of Borromini’s San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane, regarded by some art historians as the greatest building in all of Western art. Here, Borromini’s use of complex geometry is in full force, resulting in an exhilarating architectural encounter. This short walk through history has one more stop, at Santa Maria della Vittoria, before backtracking to the Palazzo Barberini, where Interior details of Borromini’s San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane in Rome both artists were working side by side, simultaneously, as they faced the same design challenge. Stehr’s 50-minute illustrated lecture on Saturday, March 9 will begin at 6 p.m.. Doors open at 5:30. $20 per person at the door. Cash only please.

pages.text: Wednesday, February 21, 2024 19 The Musical Gourmet Fast food…then and now By Joseph Gold We are going out to eat. We have to hurry because all the restaurants will be closed in Pompeii after August 24, 79AD. When we go out to a ball game or a show someplace, there are food vendors everywhere. Think of all of the food trucks and fastfood chains that we all know and love. Perhaps you already have in mind some of your favorite foods, like hotdogs and hamburgers, potato chips, and French fries, popcorn, and chocolate. Don’t forget the ketchup and the salt. But we are now finding out that the ancient Romans enjoyed the good life also. When Mt. Vesuvius erupted, it essentially froze the civilization in Pompeii and neighboring cities in place. We are The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet lucky that archaeologists are discovering new things all the time. It turns out that fast food joints are nothing new. Pompeii had at least 90 of these fast-food places. Let’s take a look back in time and get the picture as it was. Considering that Pompeii had about 90 fast food places, that’s practically one at every intersection. In many ways, these fast food restaurants were kind of like the restaurant buffets we have today. They were usually L-shaped or square with the food on display and somebody behind the counter to manage the restaurant and serve the food. The menu was proudly displayed on the wall in the form of a fresco. They had cash registers of sorts, looking more like a bowl filled with coins. And just like today, there was crime. The tough guys ate at the fast-food joints. The wealthy folks, known as patricians, dined at home. There was no ketchup, but the Romans smacked their lips with a stinky fermented fish sauce. Vinegar was used frequently, and so was honey and local herbs. There was no sugar and very little salt. These things were just too expensive. For main courses they had pork, goat, lots of grain and legumes, and they even had ice cream. Some of the popular delicacies will sound very strange to us. For instance, they loved honey roasted rodents, and flamingo tongues. For drinks, they had many forms of wine, and if the wine soured, they could refresh it with water and spices. “Hey waiter… Hurry up. I’ve got to get to the show. My favorite gladiator team is fighting for the world championship.” They sure knew how to enjoy their lives. They had to. Back then you were lucky if you lived to be 33 years old. articles.text: The Holdovers, put simply, is an extraordinary film, nominated by the Academy for a 2024 Oscar for Best Picture. From the first frame, it reminds audiences that movies are a remarkable medium for telling stories that convey an almost magical depth and breath when examining the human condition. It also possesses a deep bench of gifted actors, led by the genius of Paul Giamatti, nominated for Best Actor in a Leading Role. He inhabits the character Paul Hunham, a classics teacher at a New England boarding school. The year is 1970. He is considered by students and faculty to be a dedicated curmudgeon who long ago abandoned his conviction that he could make a difference in the lives of his students, whom he calls “troglodytes” and “smarmy Visigoths.” There is a sadness to the delight he seems to take in dropping graded blue book exams on their desks, most with large Fs and Ds. The narrative begins in earnest when Paul is called to the office of the headmaster and told that the Christmas holiday is approaching and during this two-week hiatus four students – who for various reasons – must remain at the school. They’re referred to as the “Holdovers.” Having no family, Paul is asked to watch over them, much to his consternation. As the school empties and parents arrive to pick up their sons, Dominic Sessa, Paul Giamatti, and Da’Vine Joy Randolph in The Holdovers Paul gathers his four charges in the library, and takes some pleasure in notifying them that they will use the two weeks for studying, meaning preparing for the next semester. While he is ignoring their groans and protests, a fifth student, senior Angus Tully, wonderfully portrayed by Dominic Sessa, walks in with his suitcase, clearly angrier than his usual mien. He has just received a phone call from his mother informing him that he will remain at school while she goes to St. Kits with her new husband. And so begins what becomes a road trip to Boston, one that includes the school’s food manager/cook, Mary, played by D’Vine Joy Randolph, who has been nominated for Best Actress in a Supporting Role. Also included is sharp-tongued student Angus, feeling abandoned, and of course Paul, driving his worn, nondescript sedan. The other four holdover students have been liberated, unexpectedly, by a wealthy parent of one of the boys, who arrives in a helicopter. The journey is nuanced, comical, and revelatory, focused almost completely on the bad-tempered, sullen then gradually transformative relationship between Angus and Paul. The Holdovers is beautifully written, superbly acted, and now streaming. The Holdovers. Directed by Alexander Payne. Starring Paul Giamatti, D’Vine Joy Randolph, Dominic Sessa. 2 hrs., 13 min. articles.text: The Marvel Studio/Universe franchise has earned $13.5 billion at the global box office over the past 10 years. It’s been a remarkable run wherein narratives were lifted from the pages of comic books that possessed a superhero. These are characters possessed of superhuman powers who use their abilities to triumph over evil in the form of some equally classic antagonists. Kids and many adults love this stuff. And now arrives on the big screen a lush, beautifully costumed big screen movie of sweeping vistas and stunning scenes, the Black Panther/T’Challa (Chadwick Boseman), a superhero who appeared for the first time in the 2016 Captain America: Civil War. In this incarnation, he has A scene from From Up on Poppy Hill From Up on Poppy Hill was written by Hayao Miyazaki, the father of director Goro Miyazaki, and is based on the manga story by Tetsuro Sayama. Absent the fantastical, devoid of that floating sense of the surreal so often embedded in Studio Ghibli’s animated features, Poppy Hill is a touching, straight-forward, unsentimental coming-of-age story about a strong-willed 16-year-old girl named Umi (Sarah Bolger) who meets and becomes much enamored with Shun (Anton Melchin), a member of a geeky group of boys who inhabit an aging wreck of a building out of which they run a newspaper. He is the editor. The story is set in Yokohama, overlooking a sweeping bay. The year is 1963, and Japan is only just beginning to fully emerge from the devastation of World War II. Umi, whose father was lost at sea, and whose mother is presently studying in America, helps her grandmother (Jamie Lee Curtis) run a boarding house. She is responsible for much of the cleaning and shopping while attending a nearby high school and struggling to keep up with her schoolwork. In the opening scenes, we see Umi raising a flag in homage to her greatly missed father. She is spotted by Shun who is working on his father’s tugboat. Umi soon meets Shun and learns about his and his friends’ resistance to the razing of an old building they occupy as part of urban renewal. The struggle is between reverence for the past and the urge by officials to move toward a new, more modern Japan. The Olympic Games are slated to arrive in Japan in 1964. Umi joins Shun and friends in a campaign protesting the removal of the building and the more time she and Shun spend together the deeper their connection grows. It’s been a remarkable run wherein narratives were lifted from the pages of comic books that possessed a superhero. These are characters possessed of superhuman powers who use their abilities to triumph over evil in the form of some equally classic antagonists. Kids and many adults love this stuff. And now arrives on the big screen a lush, beautifully costumed big screen movie of sweeping vistas and stunning scenes, the Black Panther/T’Challa (Chadwick Boseman), a superhero who appeared for the first time in the 2016 Captain America: Civil War. In this incarnation, he has returned to his African nation, Wakanda, to claim the throne of his father. He is prepared to take on the role of the protector of his country as the Black Panther, a man possessed of extraordinary gifts of intelligence and strength. He is welcomed home by his mother, Ramonda (Angela Bassett), and his younger sister, Shuri (Letitia Wright), both royalty. Shuri is, to the story’s delight, a techie who uses Wakanda’s magical resource, vibranium, a metal that allows Wakanda to not only be secreted in the heart of Africa, but to develop a technology that has enriched it beyond imagination. Absent the fantastical, devoid of that floating sense of the surreal so often embedded in Studio Ghibli’s animated features, Poppy Hill is a touching, straight-forward, unsentimental coming-of-age story about a strong-willed 16-year-old girl named Umi (Sarah Bolger) who meets and becomes much enamored with Shun (Anton Melchin), a member of a geeky group of boys who inhabit an aging wreck of a building out of which they run a newspaper. articles.text: On a recent Sunday with howling winds and an impending level 4 storm, 18 intrepid members of the Piedmont Seniors ventured to see Hello, Gorgeous!, a live tribute to Barbra Streisand at the Lesher Theatre in Walnut Creek. Though it was a very stormy day, the group felt fortunate that the power remained on throughout the performance. Hello, Gorgeous! is a sentimental journey starring Rebecca Clark, who portrays the vocalist-actress Barbra Streisand. She did an excellent impersonation of Streisand, belting out such favorite tunes from Funny Girl, A Star Is Born, and Yentl, as well as many of Streisand’s greatest hits such as Evergreen, The Way We Were, Second Hand Rose, You Don’t Bring Me Flowers, Memories, and many others. When Clark spoke to the audience, she even offered the same mannerisms and speech patterns as Streisand. Clark is no newcomer to show business. Like Streisand, she is also a native New Yorker, and has performed at The Aladdin and The Bellagio in Las Vegas, the Cannes Music Festival in France, and has toured with Bob Hope USO shows throughout Europe. Prior to the performance, the Piedmont Seniors enjoyed a delicious Italian lunch at Tomatina’s in downtown Walnut Creek. If you are interested in participating in either excursions or meetings of the Piedmont Seniors, contact Janet Epstein the Coordinator at jepstein@ piedmont.ca.gov. The Piedmont Seniors meet monthly at 10 a.m. at the Piedmont Community Hall on the fourth Wednesday of each month. This is in addition to optional monthly excursions to museums and varied points of interest throughout the Bay Area. You do not need to be a Piedmont resident to join.

articles.text: While some people express a desire to be “treated with dignity”, and others plead to have dignity “maintained,” it’s not always clear what this means in practical terms. There are six definitions for dignity in the dictionary, and the word can start to sound a bit posh. Perhaps this one seems to be the most relevant: “bearing, conduct, or speech indicative of self-respect or appreciation of the formality or gravity of any occasion or situation.” Another way of putting it would be that one person’s actions show they care about another. “To me, dignity means a recognition of the person: as valued, and as an equal in any interactions, regardless of any infirmity or disability,” says Dr. G. Allen Power, M.D., a geriatrician, dementia expert and author of “Dementia Beyond Drugs: Changing the Culture of Care.” “It means recognizing that all people have certain basic rights. In the case of health care, these include the right to be informed of one’s medical diagnoses, the right to make choices regarding not only treatment decisions, but also all aspects of daily living,” he says. Treating people with dignity extends to those who no longer seem able to self-advocate. “Dignity also means recognizing older people and those living with dementia as adults; not infantilizing, talking down to, or seeing them as childlike,” Dr. Power says. “We support our parents and assist them to be as capable as possible, but we do not “parent” them.” Easier said than done Treating people with kindness and caring seems obvious and simple, but one man’s dignity is another man’s insult. Pride and dignity, while distinctly different feelings, can be in conflict when a person has to rely on another in some capacity. “There are many societal stigmas around both aging and dementia,” Dr. Power explains. “Society tends to value older people less than those who are younger and who are gainfully employed. We also attach a great deal of worth to our cognitive abilities, and those who are less able are devalued and marginalized.” Within society is a complex healthcare system that, according to Dr. Power, does not always set up people for dignified moments. “Our care systems that are more focused on tasks than people and are often very rigid,” he says. “As a result, the desires and needs of the individual are often lost in an inflexible care system, and many of the practices that result also rob people of their dignity. A perfect example is rotating care staff at our convenience, which subjects people to receiving showers and other personal care from a parade of strangers.” Dementia can add another layer of challenges for all parties when striving for dignity. “There are many myths and stigmas around dementia that fuel people’s fears, and lead them to believe that the person is “fading away,” is incapable of being engaged meaningfully, or having input and choice in daily living. These beliefs set up a series of self-fulfilling prophecies, where we expect less of people and therefore do not provide an environment in which they can be more, and then their inability to do more reinforces our view that they are incapable,” he says. Give It a Try If you have a loved one who needs care and are concerned about respecting their dignity, try Dr. Power’s suggestions for how to consciously treat them with the decency that they want: • Learn and use optimal communication techniques so that people are well understood and can understand you. There are six definitions for dignity in the dictionary, and the word can start to sound a bit posh. Perhaps this one seems to be the most relevant: “bearing, conduct, or speech indicative of self-respect or appreciation of the formality or gravity of any occasion or situation.” Another way of putting it would be that one person’s actions show they care about another. “To me, dignity means a recognition of the person: as valued, and as an equal in any interactions, regardless of any infirmity or disability,” says Dr. G. Allen Power, M.D., a geriatrician, dementia expert and author of “Dementia Beyond Drugs: Changing the Culture of Care.” “It means recognizing that all people have certain basic rights. In the case of health care, these include the right to be informed of one’s medical diagnoses, the right to make choices regarding not only treatment decisions, but also all aspects of daily living,” he says. Treating people with dignity extends to those who no longer seem able to self-advocate. “Dignity also means recognizing older people and those living with dementia as adults; not infantilizing, talking down to, or seeing them as childlike,” Dr. Power says. “We support our parents and assist them to be as capable as possible, but we do not “parent” them.” Easier said than done Treating people with kindness and caring seems obvious and simple, but one man’s dignity is another man’s insult. Pride and dignity, while distinctly different feelings, can be in conflict when a person has to rely on another in some capacity. “There are many societal stigmas around both aging and dementia,” Dr. Power explains. “Society tends to value older people less than those who are younger and who are gainfully employed. We also attach a great deal of worth to our cognitive abilities, and those who are less able are devalued and marginalized.” Within society is a complex healthcare system that, according to Dr. Power, does not always set up people for dignified moments. “Our care systems that are more focused on tasks than people and are often very rigid,” he says. “As a result, the desires and needs of the individual are often lost in an inflexible care system, and many of the practices that result also rob people of their dignity. A perfect example is rotating care staff at our convenience, which subjects people to receiving showers and other personal care from a parade of strangers.” Dementia can add another layer of challenges for all parties when striving for dignity. “There are many myths and stigmas around dementia that fuel people’s fears, and lead them to believe that the person is “fading away,” is incapable of being engaged meaningfully, or having input and choice in daily living. By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama: I am trying to get my estate in order so I can update my trust. One of my friends recommended I keep myself organized on my computer. I have no idea how to even get started. My attorney wants my updated beneficiary list and changes. How do I begin? -Lissa R., Oakland Dear Lissa: When you realize how valuable a tool a computer can be to get yourself organized for things like managing your beneficiary list for your trust and will, managing your medical expenses, etc., it helps with the stress of getting ready for the inevitable. Since I am assuming you don’t plan to try to create your will and trust by yourself without an attorney, here are some ways to get organized. 1. Create a folder for all of the documents you need and create You might label it Trust and Will 2024. In this folder, you can keep scanned documents to help you get organized, bank account, account, numbers, and any documents that you create. 2. Get your documents in order It’s very likely that your financial planner or stockbroker has a guide how to organize your documents to make it easier for your executor or family members to proceed in the event of your death. You should organize things like investment accounts, bank, accounts, and assets. If you are making a trust for the first time, you should know the limits of what you can have before things go to probate. If you have a lot of money in your checking account, for example, you should make sure it doesn’t exceed the limit to necessitate probate. Assets are subject to probate if they are not in trust, jointly held, or if a beneficiary designation is not in place. As a reference, decedent estates had to be probated when assets subject to probate exceeded $184,500 for persons who passed away in 2023. And assets aggregate maximum value threshold for 2023 was $25,000. Each item’s value cannot exceed $5000. So if you have artwork worth more than $5000 apiece, you want make sure that is put in the trust. Again, it’s important to talk to your financial advisor about the state of your accounts. You can keep copies of investment statements, bank statements, etc. in your organizational folder. 3. Create a spreadsheet Your Mac comes with spreadsheet, word processor, and presentation software. The spreadsheet software is called Numbers. Of course, many of us have Microsoft products, and that case you can use Excel if you have that on your computer. Then you can make headings for the types of beneficiaries that you may have. The headings can be family, friends, and nonprofits and charities. For the nonprofits and charities, you will need their addresses, their EIN numbers phone numbers and or email. If you’re not even sure which charities to choose, you can use a well-known site like charitynavigator.org. This very useful site gives you ratings for the charities, as well as all of their contact and Tax ID information. There are also some nonprofit groups on this site. For personal beneficiaries, it’s a good idea to have addresses, phone numbers, and current email addresses. A spreadsheet is also incredibly useful to list your investment and bank account, their numbers, who the beneficiaries are, and contact info for customer support whether it be your financial advisor or bank representative. 4. Talk to your family members This sounds easy, but it’s often very difficult to talk to your children or relatives who will be handling your estate upon your death. But it’s a necessary conversation. Who will be the executor? It’s not an easy job and it takes somebody that can persevere in dealing with beneficiary, payouts, sale of property of necessary, etc. You also want to make sure that you have medical and durable power of attorney in place. You also must make sure that your family members that will be handling your estate have access to your passwords, bank account, and can actually get into your computer. You can create what’s known as a legacy contact on your iCloud account, this would allow these contacts, usually relatives, to have access to all of your Apple iCloud data after your death. You can also share your folder with family members through Google Drive or Dropbox 5. Fill out a Healthcare Directive and Memorial Plan This is an important aspect of trust and will planning. In a healthcare directive, you are determining how you would like to be treated if your condition becomes terminal. It’s important that your children or relatives have a copy of this, and they understand your wishes. A memorial plan indicates how you would like your remains to be handled whether for example burial with a service, cremation, or donation to science. These documented wishes should also be kept in your trust and will folder. Planning for our inevitable demise is uncomfortable, but the more that you do now, the less your beneficiaries will have to deal with after your death. If you find it difficult to talk with your family members alone, you can do that with your financial advisor and family all together.
